questions.prompt: Which core MLOps concern carries over directly and unchanged to LLM systems?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: Versioning, a registry of what's deployed, monitoring, and a rollback plan — the entire core operational discipline

The fundamental operational discipline from MLOps — versioning, registries, monitoring, rollback — applies just as much to LLM-based systems as to classical ML.
keyPoints: The fundamental operational discipline from MLOps — versioning, registries, monitoring, rollback — applies just as much to LLM-based systems as to classical ML.

questions.prompt: What specific gap does the prompt-management module (module 1) address?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: The need for prompts to have their own registry, versioning, and testing discipline, since they change independently of and more often than model retraining

Prompt management directly fills the gap identified earlier in this module: prompts need dedicated versioning treatment that a classical ML model registry wasn't designed to provide.
keyPoints: Prompt management directly fills the gap identified earlier in this module: prompts need dedicated versioning treatment that a classical ML model registry wasn't designed to provide.

questions.prompt: How does prompt A/B testing extend the MLOps course's canary deployment concept?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: It builds on canary's traffic-splitting approach but usually wants a genuine statistical comparison of which version performs better, not just detecting an obviously broken new version

Prompt A/B testing uses the same traffic-splitting infrastructure as canary deployment, but adds the goal of a genuine comparative measurement rather than just catching an obviously broken version.
keyPoints: Prompt A/B testing uses the same traffic-splitting infrastructure as canary deployment, but adds the goal of a genuine comparative measurement rather than just catching an obviously broken version.

questions.prompt: What does a span represent in an LLM tracing system?
questions.referenceAnswer:
Answer: One discrete step in the overall request (a model call, a retrieval, a tool call), with its own timing and inputs/outputs

Spans are the basic building block of a trace, capturing individual steps with their own timing and data, which nest and sequence together to form the full request trace.
keyPoints: Spans are the basic building block of a trace, capturing individual steps with their own timing and data, which nest and sequence together to form the full request trace.

questions.prompt: What does a representative test-case set for an LLM evaluation harness build on from earlier courses?
questions.referenceAnswer: This harness directly extends the held-out and eval-set-building principles already established in the Fine-Tuning and RAG courses, rather than introducing an unrelated new concept.
keyPoints: This harness directly extends the held-out and eval-set-building principles already established in the Fine-Tuning and RAG courses, rather than introducing an unrelated new concept.

The LangGraph course's state schema design principles

questions.prompt: What does a complete deployment gate for an LLM application change need to check, per this lesson?
questions.referenceAnswer: A complete gate checks multiple dimensions together (quality, regression, cost/latency), directly implementing the multi-dimensional evaluation principle from this course's fundamentals module.
keyPoints: A complete gate checks multiple dimensions together (quality, regression, cost/latency), directly implementing the multi-dimensional evaluation principle from this course's fundamentals module.

choices.text: Only whether the change improves the target evaluation metric, with no other checks needed
Whether it clears a quality bar, passes the regression suite, and stays within cost/latency bounds — all together, not just one dimension

questions.prompt: Why doesn't hallucination detection map cleanly onto the MLOps course's drift-detection approach?
questions.referenceAnswer: Hallucination's lack of a clean ground-truth or input-distribution comparison point (especially for open-ended generation) is exactly why it needs its own detection approaches rather than reusing MLOps drift detection directly.
keyPoints: Hallucination's lack of a clean ground-truth or input-distribution comparison point (especially for open-ended generation) is exactly why it needs its own detection approaches rather than reusing MLOps drift detection directly.

choices.text: Hallucination and drift are actually identical phenomena with the same detection method

Drift detection relies on comparing production data to training data or predictions to ground truth, but hallucination lacks a clean equivalent, especially for open-ended queries with no single retrievable correct answer
Hallucination never actually occurs in production LLM systems
Drift detection techniques work perfectly for detecting hallucination with no modification needed

questions.prompt: Why do LLM applications need explicit, measurable SLOs rather than a vague 'be fast' goal?
questions.referenceAnswer: The unpredictability of LLM generation latency compared to typical software makes a concrete, measurable target more necessary than it might be for more predictable systems.
keyPoints: The unpredictability of LLM generation latency compared to typical software makes a concrete, measurable target more necessary than it might be for more predictable systems.

choices.text: Vague goals are always sufficient for any software system
Generation latency scales with output length and model size in a way that's less predictable than typical software response times, making a concrete measured target necessary
LLM applications never actually have any latency concerns
SLOs are only relevant for classical ML systems, never LLM-based ones

questions.prompt: A new prompt release lowers quality for one customer group. What would you inspect first, and why?
questions.referenceAnswer: Compare cohorts against the previous prompt version. Inspect regression cases and model settings. Roll back the version while evaluating a fix on held-out cases.
keyPoints: Compare cohorts against the previous prompt version.
Inspect regression cases and model settings.
Roll back the version while evaluating a fix on held-out cases.

questions.prompt: How would you test that the change fixed this incident rather than hiding it?
questions.referenceAnswer: Keep a reproducible failing case for this incident. Roll back the version while evaluating a fix on held-out cases. Compare the same workload before and after the change; record both the target metric and regressions.
keyPoints: Roll back the version while evaluating a fix on held-out cases.
Compare the same workload before and after the change.
Check regressions as well as the target metric.

questions.prompt: The fix works in a small test but fails at production scale. What next?
questions.referenceAnswer: Compare cohorts against the previous prompt version. Measure representative workloads and separate resource, data and configuration differences. Stage a rollout with a rollback condition and rerun the original failure case.
keyPoints: Compare cohorts against the previous prompt version.
Measure a representative workload.
Stage rollout and define rollback criteria.
